This guide explains what CTET Whole Numbers actually tests, the facts worth memorising, the mistakes that quietly cost marks, and a free 10-question online test you can take right now to see where you stand.

Take the quiz below first, read the explanation for anything you miss, then use the chapter e-book at the end for full, exam-level practice.

What CTET Paper 2 asks on Whole Numbers

Questions cover the number line, successor and predecessor, and the properties of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division — closure, commutativity, associativity, identity and the distributive law.

Key facts & formulas to remember

  • Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, … ; 0 is the smallest and there is no largest.
  • Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative on whole numbers; subtraction and division are not.
  • Additive identity is 0 (a + 0 = a); multiplicative identity is 1 (a × 1 = a).
  • Distributive law: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.
  • Every whole number except 0 has a predecessor; every one has a successor.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming subtraction or division is commutative (7 − 3 ≠ 3 − 7).
  • Thinking 0 is a natural number (it is a whole number, not a natural number).
  • Forgetting that multiplying any number by 0 gives 0.

quiz.title: CTET Whole Numbers Practice Quiz
quiz.intro: Ten CTET Paper II–pattern questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which of the following is the smallest whole number?
questions.explanation: Whole numbers start from 0 and include all natural numbers. Hence, 0 is the smallest whole number.

questions.q: What is the successor of 5 in the set of whole numbers?
questions.explanation: The successor of a number is the next number in the sequence. For 5, the successor is 6.

questions.q: Which property is illustrated by the equation: 7 + 0 = 7?
questions.explanation: The identity property states that adding 0 to any number leaves the number unchanged.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a whole number?
questions.explanation: Whole numbers are non-negative integers. -5 is a negative integer and hence not a whole number.

questions.q: What is the predecessor of 10 in the set of whole numbers?
questions.explanation: The predecessor of a number is the number that comes just before it. For 10, the predecessor is 9.

questions.q: Which property is illustrated by the equation: (5 + 7) + 3 = 5 + (7 + 3)?
questions.explanation: The associative property states that the way in which numbers are grouped in addition does not change their sum.
Using BODMAS: first solve the bracket, (8 - 4) = 4. Then division: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Then multiplication: 3 × 2 = 6. Finally addition: 6 + 6 = 12.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of the distributive property?
questions.explanation: The distributive property states that multiplication distributes over addition: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c). This is exactly demonstrated by 5 × (3 + 4) = (5 × 3) + (5 × 4).

questions.q: If a student thinks that 0 is not a whole number, which misconception are they likely to have?
options: Not knowing the definition of whole numbers
Confusing whole numbers with natural numbers
questions.explanation: Students often confuse whole numbers (0, 1, 2, ...) with natural numbers (1, 2, 3, ...), excluding 0 from the former.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example to teach the closure property of addition for whole numbers?
questions.explanation: The closure property states that the sum of any two whole numbers is also a whole number. 3 + 4 = 7 is a simple and clear example.

faq.q: Are whole numbers and natural numbers the same?
faq.a: No. Natural numbers start at 1; whole numbers include 0 as well (0, 1, 2, 3, …).

faq.q: Why is the distributive law important?
faq.a: It links multiplication and addition and underpins mental-maths strategies and later algebra — a common CTET pedagogy theme.
